title: The 2026 global power market outlook: common problems, diverse solutions
gist: Wood Mackenzie's 2026 global power outlook finds common pressures (data-centre and electrification demand, grid constraints, Middle East energy-security risk) met with diverse regional strategies: an all-of-the-above, gas-heavy US; a Europe that decarbonises fast but misses targets; a slower-growing, renewables-and-battery-led Southern Cone; and APAC driving nearly three-quarters of global demand growth to 2035.

insights.claim: Electricity demand continues to grow globally, driven by industrialisation, electrification and rapid data centre buildout, while infrastructure struggles to keep up in many markets.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Grid and generation shortfalls create investment demand across regions.

insights.claim: The Middle East conflict has heightened energy security concerns that threaten to structurally reshape power market dynamics.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Geopolitics is now a structural driver of power-market design and fuel choices.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts US power sales growing 3.2% per year through 2035, with two-thirds of that growth from data centres, even as the data centre pipeline growth slows.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Data centres dominate US load growth, supporting utilities and generation builders.
insights.quote: we now forecast 3.2% annual sales growth through 2035, two-thirds of which will come from datacentres
insights.locator: Data centre pipeline growth is slowing

insights.claim: Canadian power demand growth is expected at 2.2% annually through 2035, up from 1.5% in the previous outlook.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Upward revision improves Canadian utility growth outlook.
insights.locator: Data centre pipeline growth is slowing

insights.claim: Gas is expected to contribute 52% of incremental US generation through 2035 given the current administration's support, leading to rising emissions in all major US markets.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Gas turbines and pipelines benefit, while emissions rise.
insights.locator: The popularity of gas with the current

insights.claim: With US gas investment costs at an all-time high, the need for electrons must be balanced against stranded asset risk.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Record gas capex raises stranded-asset risk for new gas plants.
insights.quote: with gas investment costs at an all-time high, the need for electrons must be balanced against the risk of stranded assets
insights.locator: The popularity of gas with the current

insights.claim: Tension between speed to power and affordability is spurring US regional market reforms, but state responses are fragmented and there is no silver bullet, including colocation and behind-the-meter arrangements.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Large-load interconnection and cost allocation remain unresolved, a key risk for data-centre power deals.
insights.quote: there is no silver bullet - colocation and behind-the-meter arrangements included
insights.locator: The tension between speed to power

insights.claim: In North America, coal generation can expect greater longevity while renewables and storage buildout continues, but grid constraints, policy risk and affordability are limits.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Coal retirements may be delayed, extending coal asset lives.

insights.claim: Meeting Europe's demand growth will require over 1,400 GW of net new PV and wind capacity by mid-century, with battery storage surging tenfold to 470 GW by 2050 as variable renewables rise from 28% to 68% of the mix.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Defines a very large multi-decade European renewables and storage capex runway.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie projects Europe's 2030 renewables share at just below 64%, missing the REPowerEU 69% goal.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Target miss may drive additional policy support.

insights.claim: Coal will fully exit the EU27 power mix at the start of the 2040s, CCS will gain traction in the late 2030s, and gas generation declines 45% by 2050 even as installed capacity grows.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Gas fleet economics shift toward capacity/flexibility as utilisation collapses.

insights.claim: Day-ahead wholesale price support in Europe is expected in the second half of the 2030s and first half of the 2040s, offering stability to renewable owners currently suffering low capture rates.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Merchant renewable returns may improve after 2035.
insights.locator: The timing of load growth matters

insights.claim: An increasingly pro-nuclear regulatory landscape is underpinning operational extensions of Europe's existing nuclear fleet.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Supports nuclear operators' asset lives.

insights.claim: Weak investment and constrained macro policy space mean electricity demand growth in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Chile will remain below the global average.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Limits load-growth upside for Southern Cone power investments.

insights.claim: Battery storage is the Southern Cone's fastest-growing technology, while high curtailment and grid constraints create headwinds for solar and wind, particularly in Chile and Brazil.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Storage is the clear growth segment in the region.

insights.claim: Renewables will exceed 55% of Bolivia's installed capacity by 2060, limiting gas generation and weakening domestic gas monetisation.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Negative for Bolivian domestic gas demand.

insights.claim: In Brazil hydro water availability is the main price uncertainty, with marginal costs likely rising between 2029 and 2040 as large-load demand accelerates; Argentina's June-August marginal costs are projected to reach US$100/MWh by 2060.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Rising marginal costs support thermal and storage economics in these markets.

insights.claim: Gas retains a dispatchable role in all four Southern Cone markets, though battery flexibility will support more renewables and erode gas's share in Argentina after 2040.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Gas remains a reliability backstop, but long-run share declines.

insights.claim: APAC will account for nearly three-quarters of global electricity demand growth to 2035, driven by China, India and Southeast Asia.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: APAC is the center of gravity for global power investment.

insights.claim: China's power demand exceeded 10,000 TWh in 2025, the first country to reach that milestone, and China holds 72% of APAC's installed capacity.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: China's scale dominates regional equipment and fuel demand.

insights.claim: Chinese coal-fired capacity should peak by 2030 and shift to a flexibility role, though coal will dominate marginal prices through 2035.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Peak Chinese coal capacity signals long-run thermal coal demand plateau.

insights.claim: Wind and solar are 47% of China's power capacity and will rise to 84% by 2060 (73% of generation), with energy storage expanding 8.5% annually.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Long runway for Chinese renewables and storage manufacturers.

insights.claim: Australia's power system is set to triple capacity by 2060, but grid, transmission and delivery constraints mean renewables will lag the 82% renewable generation target for 2030.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Australian renewable targets at risk; grid buildout is the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects full coal retirement in Australia in 2047, with gas remaining a residual balancing resource through 2060.
insights.speaker: Brian Gaylord
insights.so_what: Coal and gas stay higher for longer, supporting incumbent thermal assets.
